paras: The Rose Hill attempted lynching was an attempt by citizens in early June 1881 to lynch one of three white men accused of assaulting a blacksmith's daughter at Rose Hill, Lee County, apparently in Virginia. After capturing the man across the state line in Tennessee, his pursuers brought him back to the scene of the crime and prepared to lynch him; the only report does not say what followed.

According to a brief in The Meridional of Abbeville, Louisiana, three white men went one night "last week" to the house of a blacksmith named Rosier at Rose Hill, saying they had come to spend a friendly evening with the family. The brief gives the state as "Vie.", most likely a misprint or misreading of "Va." The family received them well, but the men are said to have drawn revolvers, forced Rosier and his wife into a corner and held them there while they in turn assaulted the couple's nineteen-year-old daughter.

The three men then fled across the state line into Tennessee. Citizens soon pursued them and captured one, whose name is not given. They took him back to the scene of the crime, the blacksmith's house, and "immediately" made the preparations needed to lynch him. The brief ends there, and no later report of whether he was killed, released or handed to the authorities appears in the coverage.
No report of the capture of the other two men, of an inquest or of a trial appears in the coverage.

The episode is known from a single French-language item in The Meridional on 11 June 1881, printed on the front page. Headed "Un crime révoltant", it called the accused "les lâches" (the cowards) and reported the lynching preparations without comment for or against. No other report of the case, in English or in the Black press, appears in the coverage.
